title: The useless tree
hook: a giant oak survives every axe because its wood is good for nothing (Zhuangzi 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cook Ding's knife stayed sharp for nineteen years by sliding through the spaces. Your line was find the gaps. Where did you find one? Day fifty-two.

How was your week? Busy? Productive? We measure ourselves by use. What did you get done. What are you good for. Even rest gets sold to us as a way to be more productive later. Now, in the book of Zhuangzi, a master carpenter named Shi is traveling with his apprentice, and they pass a village shrine with the biggest tree anyone has ever seen. An oak, the translators usually say, wide enough to shade thousands of oxen. Crowds come just to stare at it. And the master carpenter walks right past without a glance. Today's story is the useless tree.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU GOOD FOR?` → `CARPENTER SHI AND HIS APPRENTICE.` → `HE WALKS RIGHT PAST.`

segments.voice: The apprentice runs to catch up. Master, I've never seen timber like that. Why didn't you even look? And the carpenter says: forget it. That tree's worthless. Make a boat from it, and it sinks. A coffin, and it rots. A tool, and it breaks. A door, and it oozes sap. A pillar, and the worms get in. It's good for nothing. That's why it's grown so old. That night, the tree appears to the carpenter in a dream. And it's not pleased. What were you comparing me to, it asks? The useful trees? The pear, the orange, the ones with fruit? The moment their fruit is ripe, they're stripped and their branches torn. Their usefulness makes their life bitter, and they don't live out their years. I've been working at being useless for a very long time, the tree says. And it has been of great use to me. If I'd been useful, would I ever have grown this big? The chapter ends with a line people still quote: everyone knows the usefulness of the useful. Nobody knows the usefulness of the useless. Now, Zhuangzi isn't telling anyone to stop working. He's poking at a habit of mind: judging everything, including people, by what it produces. The tree's shade, its shelter, the crowds who come to stand under it: none of that counts as use, to the carpenter. But it's why the tree is still alive, and why people travel to see it. Some of what matters most in a life is useless in exactly this way.
screen: `A BOAT SINKS, A COFFIN ROTS.` · `THE TREE SPEAKS IN A DREAM.` · `THE USEFUL ONES ARE STRIPPED.` · `THE USEFULNESS OF THE USELESS.` · then, large: `USELESS, AND ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: spend these two minutes useful to no one. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to get better at anything. Don't try to relax so you'll be more productive later. Don't improve. Just sit, like a big old tree nobody wants for timber. Let the breath come and go on its own. If a to-do thought appears, let it pass like a carpenter walking by. You're not here for anything. You're just alive. The bell holds the time.
Zhuangzi. The ancient thinker whose useless oak, unwanted by any carpenter, lived long enough to shelter everyone.
Your line: useless, and alive. Today, spend five minutes useful to no one: no phone, no task, no goal. Watch clouds, sit on a step, just be there. Day fifty-two.

howItsDone: Taoist tradition reads the useless tree as a teaching about the value of what can't be measured, and the Zhuangzi returns to useless trees several times, including in its first and fourth chapters.

original.note: Chinese, wú yòng zhī yòng: the usefulness of the useless, the phrase that closes Zhuangzi chapter four.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tree too bad to cut down.
what it means: judging everything by its use misses some of what matters most, and what keeps things alive.
what a scholar hears: Zhuangzi chapter four, Carpenter Shi and the shrine oak, closing on wú yòng zhī yòng, the usefulness of the useless.

sources.ref: Zhuangzi, chapter 4 (Renjianshi), Carpenter Shi and the shrine tree; closing line on the usefulness of the useless

notes: Zhuangzi 4 paraphrased closely, not quoted. The tree (櫟, li) is usually translated oak (sometimes 'serrated oak' or 'chestnut-leaved oak'); script says 'an oak, the translators usually say'.
'Wide enough to shade thousands of oxen' follows the text's hyperbole; confirm.
The closing line (人皆知有用之用，而莫知無用之用也) is at the very end of chapter 4; paraphrased. Chinese 無用之用: confirm.
The practice is sized to the 2-minute sit; the outline's 'five minutes useful to no one' is moved to the carry.
